newsitem.title: CANADA: Alcan expects strong growth for magnesium.
newsitem.headline: Alcan expects strong growth for magnesium.

text.p: Magnesium demand and recycling are set to grow at a healthy clip over coming years but producers will have to ensure responsive prices, Jocelyn Gagne of Alcan Aluminum told delegates at the International Magnesium Association annual conference.

Western world consumption growth rate from 1985 to 1995 has been 2.7 percent for magnesium and 4.3 percent for aluminum. In 1995 to 2005 Alcan forecast growth of 4.5 to 5 percent for magnesium and 4 percent for aluminum.
Western world magnesium consumption is 280,000 to 300,000 tonnes a year.
At present only 11 percent of magnesium is recycled, but this rate should start to rise significantly over coming years with magnesium penetration increasing in the transportation sector.
Die cast magnesium components for autos is the fastest growth sector for the light metal, led by North American car manufacturing.

The aluminum industry consumes over half the world's magnesium production to add strength in extrusions and canstock for beverage cans. Beverage cans alone account for a quarter of world magnesium consumption, Gagne said.
Gagne forecast world aluminum can consumption growth of 3.5 to 4 percent per annum out to 2005, largely in Latin America (Brazil and Argentina), Asia (China and India), and Europe.
"North America will probably not see any growth," Gagne said.
Thinner sheet is being used to make beverage cans and world canstock consumption will be down to 2.00 to 2.5 percent a yera.
The extensive use of aluminum sheet in autos is not expected to see any big volume until 2005, Gagne said.

He also raised the longstanding issue of whether magnesium should be traded on a futures exchange like aluminum - some magnesium consumers are unhappy with the current pricing system based on published prices in trade journals and producer lists.
But Gagne said as long as "producers behaved themselves properly", there is no need to trade magnesium on New York's COMEX or the London Metal Exchange.

"But if prices just move up and never come down then maybe we do need magnesium to be traded on COMEX or LME to provide some more transparency," Gagne said. "But so far the magnesium industry has been behaving relatively well."
Later Gagne said Alcan has not approached the futures exchanges to seek a magnesium contract, adding there remained issues to be resolved such as how well the metal could be stored in a warehouse.
